Muscle mass in adults is always being built up and broken down at the same time. In young adults the two processes cancel each other out. As you age, breakdown starts to win. After 40, you lose muscle at a rate of roughly 0.5% to 2% per year.

Researchers recently found why. A system called ubiquitin-proteasome-dependent proteinolysis, which clears out worn contractile muscle proteins, stops being properly held in check, so it degrades too much. The good news: supplementing older people with the amino acid leucine restored this system to normal working order.
rejected: Adult muscle is constantly being built up and broken down. In young adults these two processes stay roughly balanced, but aging tips that balance toward breakdown. Recent research suggests that giving older people the amino acid leucine can restore the balance. After age 40, muscle loss speeds up to about 0.5% to 2% per year. The researchers identified the mechanism as a defective inhibition of ubiquitin-proteasome-dependent proteinolysis, the degradative machinery that clears contractile muscle proteins. Leucine supplementation can fully restore the correct functioning of this system.

chosen: The upper layer of the Alboran Sea circulates through a fast Atlantic current jet that feeds two anticyclonic gyres, which rotate clockwise when seen from above in the Northern Hemisphere. Together they form the Alboran Gyre: the Western Alboran Gyre (WAG) and the Eastern Alboran Gyre (EAG). Roughly two-thirds of the Atlantic water entering the Strait of Gibraltar supplies the kinetic energy and flow of this gyre system. The circulation changes with the seasons. In summer the two-gyre system holds steady, while in winter a coastal jet, usually called the Algerian Current, runs along the African shore.
